title: The `for` Loop: Iterating Over Collections 🗂️
description: Loop through lists, strings, files – the workhorse of scanning and enumeration.

slides.title: For Loop: Python's Favorite Way to Loop
slides.content:
# `for item in iterable:`

When you have a list of targets, a wordlist, or a string, the `for` loop automatically gives you each element one by one.

```python
ips = ["192.168.1.1", "10.0.0.2", "172.16.0.5"]
for ip in ips:
    print(f"Scanning {ip}")
```
No manual index, no counter – Python handles it.

slides.title: Iterating Over Strings
slides.content:
# Strings Are Sequences of Characters

```python
banner = "SSH-2.0"
for char in banner:
    if char.isdigit():
        print(f"Digit found: {char}")
```
You can loop through each character. Useful for parsing.

quizData.explanation: Each character becomes the loop variable in turn.

slides.title: Iterating Over Files (Reading Lines)
slides.content:
# Huge for Log Parsing

You can loop over a file object to process each line:
```python
with open("passwords.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        attempt = line.strip()
        print(f"Trying {attempt}")
```
The `for` loop reads the file line by line, not loading everything into memory. Perfect for large wordlists.

slides.title: The Loop Variable Exists After the Loop
slides.content:
# Interesting Quirk

After a for loop finishes, the loop variable still holds the last value:
```python
for port in [80, 443]:
    pass
print(port)  # 443
```
Be careful not to rely on this unintentionally.

slides.title: Using `enumerate()` for Counters
slides.content:
# Need the Index Alongside the Item?

`enumerate()` gives you pairs of (index, item):
```python
targets = ["host1", "host2", "host3"]
for i, target in enumerate(targets):
    print(f"{i}: {target}")
```
No manual counter variable needed!
